claim: TPX2 is a microtubule-associated protein from multicellular eukaryotes that is nuclear during interphase.
source: Among them is TPX2 (Wittmann et al., 1998), a MAP from multicellular eukaryotes that is nuclear during interphase (Neumayer et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wittmann et al., 1998; Neumayer et al., 2012).

claim: TPX2 associates with spindle microtubules after nuclear breakdown during mitosis and meiosis.
source: Among them is TPX2 (Wittmann et al., 1998), a MAP from multicellular eukaryotes that is nuclear during interphase (Neumayer et al., 2012) and associates with spindle MTs after nuclear breakdown during mitosis and meiosis (Garrett et al., 2002; Gruss et al., 2002; Heidebrecht et al., 1997; Neumayer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Garrett et al., 2002; Gruss et al., 2002; Heidebrecht et al., 1997; Neumayer et al., 2014).

claim: Both over- and under-expression of TPX2 perturb microtubule organization, leading to genomic instability.
source: Both over- and under-expression of TPX2 perturb MT organization, leading to genomic instability, and mutations in TPX2 are correlated with high metastasis frequency in cancer patients (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2006; Gruss et al., 2002; Pérez de Castro and Malumbres, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2006; Gruss et al., 2002; Pérez de Castro and Malumbres, 2012).

claim: Mutations in TPX2 are correlated with high metastasis frequency in cancer patients.
source: Both over- and under-expression of TPX2 perturb MT organization, leading to genomic instability, and mutations in TPX2 are correlated with high metastasis frequency in cancer patients (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2006; Gruss et al., 2002; Pérez de Castro and Malumbres, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2006; Gruss et al., 2002; Pérez de Castro and Malumbres, 2012).

claim: TPX2 is a marker for the diagnosis and prognosis of malignancies.
source: Consequently, TPX2 is a marker for the diagnosis and prognosis of malignancies (Gruss et al., 2002; Heidebrecht et al., 1997; Neumayer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gruss et al., 2002; Heidebrecht et al., 1997; Neumayer et al., 2014).

claim: TPX2 is a critical component of the Ran-pathway.
source: TPX2 is a critical component of the so-called Ran-pathway (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015).

claim: Local production of Ran-GTP around mitotic and meiotic chromosomes liberates proteins containing a nuclear localization signal from the inhibitory action of importins.
source: Local production of Ran-GTP around mitotic and meiotic chromosomes liberates proteins that contain a nuclear localization signal (NLS), including a set of spindle assembly factors, from the inhibitory action of importins (nuclear transport receptors).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Ran-GTP pathway and is presented as background information.

claim: TPX2 has prominent roles in local microtubule formation around chromatin.
source: TPX2 is one such spindle assembly factor, having prominent roles in local MT formation around chromatin (Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Petry et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Petry et al., 2013).

claim: TPX2 targets other spindle components to the spindle.
source: TPX2 is one such spindle assembly factor, having prominent roles in local MT formation around chromatin (Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Petry et al., 2013) and targeting of other spindle components to the spindle (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015).

claim: The N-terminus of TPX2 interacts directly with Aurora A kinase, thereby activating and targeting Aurora A to the spindle.
source: Its N-terminus interacts directly with Aurora A kinase, thereby activating and targeting Aurora A to the spindle (Bayliss et al., 2003; Eyers et al., 2003; Giubettini et al., 2011; Kufer et al., 2002; Tsai et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Bayliss et al., 2003; Eyers et al., 2003; Giubettini et al., 2011; Kufer et al., 2002; Tsai et al., 2003).

claim: TPX2-stimulated Aurora A activity is important for proper spindle assembly, centrosome function and γ-tubulin ring complex activation.
source: TPX2-stimulated Aurora A activity is important for proper spindle assembly, centrosome function and γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) activation (Pinyol et al., 2013; Scrofani et al., 2015; Tsai and Zheng, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pinyol et al., 2013; Scrofani et al., 2015; Tsai and Zheng, 2005).

claim: The C-terminal half of TPX2 contains α-helical repeats that are important for stimulating augmin-mediated branching microtubule nucleation in Xenopus laevis egg extract.
source: The C-terminal half of TPX2 contains α-helical repeats that were shown to be important for stimulating augmin-mediated branching MT nucleation in Xenopus laevis egg extract (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Sanchez-Pulido et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Sanchez-Pulido et al., 2016).

claim: The very C-terminus of TPX2 interacts with the two mitotic kinesins Kif11/Eg5 and Kif15/Xklp2.
source: The very C-terminus of TPX2 interacts with the two mitotic kinesins Kif11/Eg5 and Kif15/Xklp2 (originally having given the protein its name: TPX2 is short for 'targeting protein for Xklp2') (Eckerdt et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2010; Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Wittmann et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Eckerdt et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2010; Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Wittmann et al., 2000).

claim: TPX2 mediates proper spindle localization of Kif11/Eg5 and Kif15/Xklp2 motors.
source: The very C-terminus of TPX2 interacts with the two mitotic kinesins Kif11/Eg5 and Kif15/Xklp2 (originally having given the protein its name: TPX2 is short for 'targeting protein for Xklp2') (Eckerdt et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2010; Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Wittmann et al., 2000), mediating proper spindle localization of these motors (Helmke and Heald, 2014; Ma et al., 2010; Wittmann et al., 1998; Wittmann et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Helmke and Heald, 2014; Ma et al., 2010; Wittmann et al., 1998; Wittmann et al., 2000).

claim: TPX2 directly promotes microtubule stability by reducing the frequency of catastrophes.
source: In vitro experiments with purified proteins have demonstrated that TPX2 directly promotes MT stability by reducing the frequency of catastrophes (transition from MT growth to depolymerization) and by slowing down depolymerization (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 directly promotes microtubule stability by slowing down depolymerization.
source: In vitro experiments with purified proteins have demonstrated that TPX2 directly promotes MT stability by reducing the frequency of catastrophes (transition from MT growth to depolymerization) and by slowing down depolymerization (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 can directly stabilize microtubule nucleation intermediates.
source: Furthermore, TPX2 can directly stabilize MT nucleation intermediates (Roostalu et al., 2015) thereby efficiently stimulating MT nucleation in pure tubulin solutions (Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015; Woodruff et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 efficiently stimulates microtubule nucleation in pure tubulin solutions.
source: Furthermore, TPX2 can directly stabilize MT nucleation intermediates (Roostalu et al., 2015) thereby efficiently stimulating MT nucleation in pure tubulin solutions (Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015; Woodruff et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015; Woodruff et al., 2017).

claim: The central portion of TPX2 contains the nuclear localization signal whose interaction with importin-α is well characterized biochemically and structurally.
source: The central portion of TPX2 also contains the NLS whose interaction with importin-α is well characterized, both biochemically and at a structural level (Giesecke and Stewart, 2010; Schatz et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Giesecke and Stewart, 2010; Schatz et al., 2003).

claim: Importins suppress TPX2 binding to microtubules in vitro.
source: Importins suppress TPX2 binding to MTs and MT nucleation in vitro (Roostalu et al., 2015; Schatz et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015; Schatz et al., 2003).

claim: Importins suppress microtubule nucleation by TPX2 in vitro.
source: Importins suppress TPX2 binding to MTs and MT nucleation in vitro (Roostalu et al., 2015; Schatz et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015; Schatz et al., 2003).

claim: TPX2 bound with higher affinity to growing microtubule ends than to the rest of the microtubule in in vitro experiments with purified proteins.
source: In in vitro experiments with purified proteins, TPX2 bound with higher affinity to growing MT ends than to the rest of the MT, a preference likely resulting from sensitivity to the characteristic nucleotide state and/or the curvature of the MT surface at MT ends (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 binds with increased affinity to microtubules grown in the presence of the non-hydrolyzable GTP analog GMPCPP.
source: Accordingly, TPX2 binds also with increased affinity to MTs grown in the presence of the non-hydrolyzable GTP analog GMPCPP (Roostalu et al., 2015), a nucleotide which is well known to stabilize MTs and to efficiently promote MT nucleation (Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: GMPCPP is well known to stabilize microtubules and to efficiently promote microtubule nucleation.
source: Accordingly, TPX2 binds also with increased affinity to MTs grown in the presence of the non-hydrolyzable GTP analog GMPCPP (Roostalu et al., 2015), a nucleotide which is well known to stabilize MTs and to efficiently promote MT nucleation (Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hyman et al., 1992).

claim: GMPCPP-microtubules have a more extended lattice structure with a slightly different lattice twist compared to GDP-microtubules.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) studies revealed that GMPCPP-MTs have a more extended lattice structure with a slightly different lattice twist compared to GDP-MTs, a conformational difference thought to reflect the more stable GTP state of the MT (Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: The central TPX2 fragment (residues 274–659) is sufficient for nucleotide and curvature-sensitive microtubule binding, albeit with reduced affinity.
source: The central TPX2 fragment (residues 274–659, Figure 1A) was shown to be sufficient for this nucleotide and curvature-sensitive MT binding, albeit with reduced affinity, and for stimulating MT nucleation, even if to a lesser extent than the full-length protein (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: The central TPX2 fragment (residues 274–659) is sufficient for stimulating microtubule nucleation, even if to a lesser extent than the full-length protein.
source: The central TPX2 fragment (residues 274–659, Figure 1A) was shown to be sufficient for this nucleotide and curvature-sensitive MT binding, albeit with reduced affinity, and for stimulating MT nucleation, even if to a lesser extent than the full-length protein (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: A 3.3 Å resolution reconstruction of mGFP-TPX2mini decorated microtubules was obtained using cryo-EM.
source: Using a MT seam search protocol that allows the structural study of MAPs with relatively small footprints on the MT lattice (Zhang and Nogales, 2015), we obtained a 3.3 Å resolution reconstruction of mGFP-TPX2mini decorated MTs (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 3A and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM reconstruction) and references to figures showing the results.

claim: The structure shows a repeating unit of two small and discontinuous densities on the microtubule surface corresponding to the TPX2mini molecule.
source: The structure shows a repeating unit of two small and discontinuous densities on the MT surface corresponding to the TPX2mini molecule (Figure 1B), which is predicted to be largely intrinsically disordered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure) and references to figures showing the results.

claim: TPX2mini is predicted to be largely intrinsically disordered.
source: The structure shows a repeating unit of two small and discontinuous densities on the MT surface corresponding to the TPX2mini molecule (Figure 1B), which is predicted to be largely intrinsically disordered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction (PSIPRED) as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ridge binds on the crest of the protofilament with an extended conformation.
source: The ridge binds on the crest of the protofilament (PF) with an extended conformation, while the wedge corresponds to a short α-helix that binds within the crevasse between two adjacent PFs and appears to be 'wedging' between neighboring tubulin subunits (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure) and references to figures showing the results.

claim: The wedge corresponds to a short α-helix that binds within the crevasse between two adjacent protofilaments.
source: The ridge binds on the crest of the protofilament (PF) with an extended conformation, while the wedge corresponds to a short α-helix that binds within the crevasse between two adjacent PFs and appears to be 'wedging' between neighboring tubulin subunits (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure) and references to figures showing the results.

claim: The absence of a connection between the ridge and wedge indicates that the linker between them is flexible and not in a fixed position with respect to the microtubule.
source: The absence of a connection between these two regions of density indicates that the linker between them is flexible and not in a fixed position with respect to the MT.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cryo-EM structure showing no density for the linker.

claim: The ridge is oriented roughly along the microtubule axis and interacts with both α- and β-tubulin across a longitudinal inter-dimer interface.
source: The ridge is oriented roughly along the MT axis and interacts with both α- and β-tubulin across a longitudinal inter-dimer interface.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure).

claim: The wedge interacts with α- and β-tubulin in one protofilament, and with another α-tubulin in the neighboring protofilament.
source: The half-buried wedge between adjacent PFs interacts also with α- and β-tubulin in one PF, and with another α-tubulin in the neighboring PF.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure).

claim: Both regions of TPX2 bind over tubulin polymerization interfaces, suggesting a potential explanation for how TPX2 can stabilize microtubules and stimulate microtubule nucleation.
source: Therefore, both regions of TPX2 bind over tubulin polymerization interfaces, suggesting a potential explanation for how TPX2 can stabilize MTs and stimulate MT nucleation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural data about TPX2 binding sites.

claim: TPX2 uses a novel mode of MAP-microtubule interaction that involves two structural elements, connected by a flexible linker, to simultaneously interact across both longitudinal and lateral tubulin dimer interfaces in the lattice.
source: Thus, TPX2 uses a novel mode of MAP-MT interaction that involves two structural elements, connected by a flexible linker, to simultaneously interact across both longitudinal and lateral tubulin dimer interfaces in the lattice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM structure) and comparison to known MAP-MT interactions.

claim: The modular microtubule engagement by TPX2 is different from previously characterized MAP-microtubule interactions, which typically involve a globular domain.
source: The modular MT engagement by TPX2 is different from previously characterized MAP-MT interactions, which typically involve a globular domain (Nogales and Zhang, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to known MAP-MT interactions cited in the literature (Nogales and Zhang, 2016).

claim: TPX2 binding is not sensitive to the exact protofilament number of microtubules.
source: Using two separate elements connected by a linker that allows for some flexibility, likely also explains why TPX2 binding is not sensitive to the exact PF number of MTs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural features of TPX2 binding.

claim: Similar binding of TPX2 was observed to GMPCPP-microtubules with either 13 or 14 protofilaments.
source: We observed similar binding to GMPCPP-MTs with either 13 or 14 PFs, which are the most typical PF numbers for these MTs polymerized in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM reconstructions) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: End binding proteins of the EB1 family and doublecortin use compact globular non-flexible domains to 'staple' across two adjacent protofilaments, resulting in a marked preference for 13-protofilament microtubules.
source: This is in contrast to end binding proteins of the EB1 family (EBs) and to the MT-stabilizing protein doublecortin (DCX), both of which use compact globular non-flexible domains to 'staple' across two adjacent PFs, resulting in a marked preference for 13-PF MTs (Fourniol et al., 2010; Maurer et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015), the typical PF number found in most cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fourniol et al., 2010; Maurer et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: The ridge corresponds to residues 300–311 of TPX2.
source: We concluded that the ridge corresponds to residues 300–311, while the wedge corresponds to residues 323–341.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (de novo modeling based on cryo-EM density map at 3.3 Å resolution).

claim: The wedge corresponds to residues 323–341 of TPX2.
source: We concluded that the ridge corresponds to residues 300–311, while the wedge corresponds to residues 323–341.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (de novo modeling based on cryo-EM density map at 3.3 Å resolution).

claim: The ridge and wedge regions of TPX2 overlap extensively with the importin-α-binding site and the nuclear localization signal of TPX2.
source: These regions overlap extensively with the importin-α-binding site and the NLS of TPX2 (Giesecke and Stewart, 2010; Schatz et al., 2003) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), directly providing a structural explanation of the inhibitory effects of importins on TPX2 (Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (atomic model) and citations to published literature (Giesecke and Stewart, 2010; Schatz et al., 2003).

claim: The mGFP-TPX2micro construct retains a strong binding preference for GMPCPP-microtubule 'seeds'.
source: TIRFM-based in vitro experiments with purified mGFP-TPX2micro and surface attached GMPCPP-MT 'seeds' from which MTs elongated in the presence of GTP, demonstrated that the shorter TPX2micro construct retains a strong binding preference for GMPCPP-MT 'seeds' (Figure 2B,C), like the longer TPX2mini, although the overall binding affinity was reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The overall binding affinity of mGFP-TPX2micro is reduced compared to TPX2mini.
source: TIRFM-based in vitro experiments with purified mGFP-TPX2micro and surface attached GMPCPP-MT 'seeds' from which MTs elongated in the presence of GTP, demonstrated that the shorter TPX2micro construct retains a strong binding preference for GMPCPP-MT 'seeds' (Figure 2B,C), like the longer TPX2mini, although the overall binding affinity was reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Cryo-EM analysis of GMPCPP-microtubules decorated with the mGFP-TPX2micro construct resulted in a reconstruction with practically identical features to the structure obtained with the longer mGFP-TPX2mini construct.
source: Cryo-EM analysis of GMPCPP-MT decorated with the mGFP-TPX2micro construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) resulted in a reconstruction with practically identical features to the structure obtained with the longer mGFP-TPX2mini construct (Figure 2D), in support of our atomic model for the ridge and the wedge elements.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (cryo-EM reconstructions) shown in Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The ridge and the wedge are connected across adjacent protofilaments by a short flexible linker of 12 residues.
source: Based on our atomic model, the ridge and the wedge are connected across adjacent PFs by a short flexible linker of 12 residues.
evidence: The claim is based on the atomic model derived from cryo-EM data.

claim: The distance that the linker between ridge and wedge could stretch roughly matches the distance between the cryo-EM densities of the ridge and the wedge.
source: The distance that this linker could stretch roughly matches the distance between the cryo-EM densities of the ridge and the wedge, but is incompatible with simultaneous binding of the two elements across the MT seam, the lattice discontinuity where α-tubulins laterally contact β-tubulins, in contrast to the rest of the lattice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the atomic model and structural constraints.

claim: The linker between ridge and wedge is incompatible with simultaneous binding of the two elements across the microtubule seam.
source: The distance that this linker could stretch roughly matches the distance between the cryo-EM densities of the ridge and the wedge, but is incompatible with simultaneous binding of the two elements across the MT seam, the lattice discontinuity where α-tubulins laterally contact β-tubulins, in contrast to the rest of the lattice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the atomic model and structural constraints.

claim: Asymmetric reconstruction of the microtubule confirmed the absence of the wedge element at the microtubule seam for TPX2mini.
source: Indeed, asymmetric (C1) reconstruction of the MT confirmed the absence of either the wedge element (for TPX2mini) or both elements (for TPX2micro) at the MT seam (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D), in further agreement with our atomic model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (asymmetric cryo-EM reconstruction) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D.

claim: Asymmetric reconstruction of the microtubule confirmed the absence of both ridge and wedge elements at the microtubule seam for TPX2micro.
source: Indeed, asymmetric (C1) reconstruction of the MT confirmed the absence of either the wedge element (for TPX2mini) or both elements (for TPX2micro) at the MT seam (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D), in further agreement with our atomic model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (asymmetric cryo-EM reconstruction) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D.

claim: The ridge of TPX2 binds the microtubule at the junction between the α:H12 and β:H11 helices in two adjacent dimers.
source: In our atomic model, the ridge of TPX2 binds the MT at the junction between the α:H12 and β:H11 helices in two adjacent dimers (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (atomic model from cryo-EM) shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ridge inserts a phenylalanine F307 into a hydrophobic pocket in tubulin defined by residues α:V435, α:Y262, α:W346 and β:R401.
source: The ridge inserts a phenylalanine F307 into a hydrophobic pocket in tubulin defined by residues α:V435, α:Y262, α:W346 and β:R401 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (atomic model from cryo-EM) shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The wedge of TPX2 interacts simultaneously with the α:H9, α:H10 and β:H6 helices in one protofilament, and α:H3 and α:H4 helices in the other protofilament.
source: The wedge of TPX2 interacts simultaneously with the α:H9, α:H10 and β:H6 helices in one PF, and α:H3 and α:H4 helices in the other PF (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (atomic model from cryo-EM) shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two residues within the wedge, F334 and H335, appear to be critical for TPX2-microtubule interaction.
source: At the interaction site with the first PF, near the inter-dimer interface, two residues within the wedge, F334 and H335, appear to be critical for TPX2-MT interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the atomic model showing these residues at the interaction interface.

claim: The identified TPX2 residues F307, F334, and H335 are conserved in organisms where TPX2 has been demonstrated to be involved in chromatin-mediated microtubule nucleation.
source: Interestingly, these identified TPX2 residues are conserved in organisms where TPX2 has been demonstrated to be involved in chromatin-mediated, that is Ran-GTP-dependent, MT nucleation (human, X. laevis, A. thaliana [Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Petrovská et al., 2013; Vos et al., 2008]), whereas they are not conserved in organisms where TPX2 appears to play no or only a minor role in this nucleation pathway, despite other involvement in correct spindle assembly (D. melanogaster, C. elegans [Hayward et al., 2014; Karsenti, 2005; Ozlü et al., 2005]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature.

claim: The identified TPX2 residues F307, F334, and H335 are not conserved in organisms where TPX2 appears to play no or only a minor role in chromatin-mediated microtubule nucleation.
source: Interestingly, these identified TPX2 residues are conserved in organisms where TPX2 has been demonstrated to be involved in chromatin-mediated, that is Ran-GTP-dependent, MT nucleation (human, X. laevis, A. thaliana [Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Petrovská et al., 2013; Vos et al., 2008]), whereas they are not conserved in organisms where TPX2 appears to play no or only a minor role in this nucleation pathway, despite other involvement in correct spindle assembly (D. melanogaster, C. elegans [Hayward et al., 2014; Karsenti, 2005; Ozlü et al., 2005]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature.

claim: Alanine replacements in either the ridge or the wedge region dramatically reduced the binding strength of mGFP-TPX2micro to GMPCPP-microtubule seeds.
source: We observed that compared to wild-type mGFP-TPX2micro (Figure 3C), alanine replacements in either the ridge or the wedge region dramatically reduced the binding strength to GMPCPP-MT seeds (Figure 3D, top and middle, respectively, 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and 3F.

claim: Simultaneous alanine replacements in both the ridge and wedge regions further reduced the microtubule interaction of the mutated TPX2micro.
source: Simultaneous alanine replacements in both binding regions further reduced the MT interaction of the mutated TPX2micro (Figure 3D, bottom, 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 3D and 3F.

claim: Glutamate replacements in the ridge or wedge regions showed an even more pronounced reduction in the binding affinity of TPX2micro compared to alanine replacements.
source: The corresponding glutamate replacements showed an even more pronounced reduction in the binding affinity (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Disrupting both the ridge and the wedge by glutamate replacements (F307E F334E H335E mutant) completely abolished all detectable microtubule binding of TPX2micro.
source: Disrupting both the ridge and the wedge by glutamate replacements (F307E F334E H335E mutant) completely abolished all detectable MT binding (Figure 3E, bottom, 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Both the ridge and the wedge are equally important for microtubule binding of TPX2.
source: These data suggest that both the ridge and the wedge are equally important for MT binding of TPX2 and strongly support the validity of the atomic model of the TPX2 MT-binding site.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mutational analysis data showing similar effects of disrupting either element.

claim: TPX2micro did not detectably bind to growing microtubule ends, probably due to its weaker overall affinity.
source: TPX2micro in contrast to TPX2mini did not detectably bind to growing MT ends, probably due to its weaker overall affinity, raising the question of whether the ridge and wedge are critical for growing MT end binding in the context of a longer TPX2 construct.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation (TIRFM assays) and inference about the reason.

claim: The F307E F334E H335E triple mutant of mGFP-TPX2mini showed abrogated binding to GMPCPP-microtubule seeds.
source: TIRFM assays with purified wild-type and mutant TPX2mini (Figure 4A,B) indeed demonstrated that binding was abrogated both to GMPCPP-MT seeds (Figure 4C) and also to growing MT ends (Figure 4D), further confirming that the novel binding module of TPX2 identified here is indeed critical for TPX2 binding to MT ends (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claim: The F307E F334E H335E triple mutant of mGFP-TPX2mini showed abrogated binding to growing microtubule ends.
source: TIRFM assays with purified wild-type and mutant TPX2mini (Figure 4A,B) indeed demonstrated that binding was abrogated both to GMPCPP-MT seeds (Figure 4C) and also to growing MT ends (Figure 4D), further confirming that the novel binding module of TPX2 identified here is indeed critical for TPX2 binding to MT ends (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM assays) shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and 4D.

claim: The novel binding module of TPX2 identified is critical for TPX2 binding to microtubule ends.
source: TIRFM assays with purified wild-type and mutant TPX2mini (Figure 4A,B) indeed demonstrated that binding was abrogated both to GMPCPP-MT seeds (Figure 4C) and also to growing MT ends (Figure 4D), further confirming that the novel binding module of TPX2 identified here is indeed critical for TPX2 binding to MT ends (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mutational analysis data showing loss of binding when the module is disrupted.

claim: Wild-type biotinylated TPX2mini strongly promoted microtubule nucleation in TIRFM-based assays.
source: Time lapse imaging revealed that the wild-type protein strongly promoted MT nucleation, as expected (Roostalu et al., 2015), whereas the MT nucleation ability of the triple mutant was severely compromised (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM-based MT nucleation assays) shown in Figure 4F and citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: The microtubule nucleation ability of the F307E F334E H335E triple mutant of biotinylated TPX2mini was severely compromised.
source: Time lapse imaging revealed that the wild-type protein strongly promoted MT nucleation, as expected (Roostalu et al., 2015), whereas the MT nucleation ability of the triple mutant was severely compromised (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (TIRFM-based MT nucleation assays) shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The identified interaction module is an important facilitator of TPX2-dependent microtubule formation.
source: This demonstrates that the identified interaction module is an important facilitator of TPX2-dependent MT formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the nucleation assay data showing reduced nucleation when the module is disrupted.

claim: TPX2 binds next to structural elements within tubulin that show significant local rearrangement during the lattice compaction that accompanies GTP hydrolysis.
source: TPX2 binds next to structural elements within tubulin that show significant local rearrangement during the lattice compaction that accompanies GTP hydrolysis (Figure 5), such as the T5 loop in β-tubulin and the H5 helix in α-tubulin (black dashed circles in Figure 5B,C) (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of cryo-EM structures and citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Binding of TPX2mini increases slightly the right-handed twist in the microtubule lattice.
source: Furthermore, comparison of the cryo-EM reconstructions of GMPCPP-MTs in the absence and presence of TPX2mini shows that binding of TPX2mini has a direct effect on the MT lattice structure. TPX2 binding increases slightly the right-handed twist in the lattice (measured as a 'dimer twist'), as well as the inter-dimer distance (measured as 'dimer rise') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (comparison of cryo-EM reconstructions) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of TPX2mini increases the inter-dimer distance in the microtubule lattice.
source: Furthermore, comparison of the cryo-EM reconstructions of GMPCPP-MTs in the absence and presence of TPX2mini shows that binding of TPX2mini has a direct effect on the MT lattice structure. TPX2 binding increases slightly the right-handed twist in the lattice (measured as a 'dimer twist'), as well as the inter-dimer distance (measured as 'dimer rise') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (comparison of cryo-EM reconstructions) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TPX2 appears to oppose the compaction of the microtubule lattice thought to occur upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: This means that TPX2 appears to oppose the compaction of the MT lattice thought to occur upon GTP hydrolysis (Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lattice parameter changes and citations to published literature (Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992).

claim: The helical character of the wedge of TPX2 may provide sufficient mechanical strength to counteract the decrease in distance between the two wedge-binding sites associated with GTP hydrolysis and lattice compaction.
source: The helical character of the wedge of TPX2 may provide sufficient mechanical strength to counteract the decrease in distance between the two wedge-binding sites (red dashed circles in Figure 5B) associated with GTP hydrolysis and lattice compaction.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the structural features of the wedge.

claim: The binding of TPX2 may lock rotamer conformations of key tubulin residues that contribute to the allosteric response to GTP hydrolysis within the tightly packed space of the microtubule lattice.
source: Moreover, the binding of TPX2 may lock rotamer conformations of key tubulin residues that contribute to the allosteric response to GTP hydrolysis within the tightly packed space of the MT lattice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on structural observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TPX2 does not only sense, but it also influences the conformational state of the microtubule.
source: These observations strongly suggest that TPX2 does not only sense, but it also influences the conformational state of the MT, suggesting a structural explanation for the MT stabilizing effect of TPX2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural observations about lattice parameter changes.

claim: Recent in vitro studies have shown that TPX2 suppresses microtubule dynamics by reducing the frequency of catastrophes and the rate of microtubule depolymerization.
source: Recent in vitro studies have shown that TPX2 suppresses MT dynamics by reducing the frequency of catastrophes and the rate of MT depolymerization (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Reid et al., 2016; Roostalu et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 promotes the elongation of the region it binds to at growing microtubule ends.
source: Furthermore, it was observed that TPX2 promotes the elongation of the region it binds to at growing MT ends (Roostalu et al., 2015), indicating that it affects conformational changes of the MT lattice, potentially suggesting that it slows down GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: End binding proteins have opposite effects on the microtubule lattice parameters compared to TPX2.
source: Remarkably, end binding proteins (EBs) have opposite effects on the MT lattice parameters (in terms of both lattice spacing and lattice twist) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Zhang et al., 2015), which is paralleled by opposite effects on the kinetics of GTPase reactions (Aguirre-Portolés et al., 2012; Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2014) and on the catastrophe frequency and nucleation efficiency of MTs as compared to TPX2 (Bieling et al., 2007; Komarova et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2015; Vitre et al., 2008; Wieczorek et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature.

claim: TPX2 contains other microtubule-binding regions that can increase its microtubule-binding affinity and may additionally contribute to its ability to stabilize microtubules.
source: In addition to the stably bound wedge and ridge elements that we see in our cryo-EM structures, TPX2 contains other MT-binding regions that can increase its MT-binding affinity and may additionally contribute to its ability to stabilize MTs (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Brunet et al., 2004; Roostalu et al., 2015; Trieselmann et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Brunet et al., 2004; Roostalu et al., 2015; Trieselmann et al., 2003).

claim: TPX2 can directly promote microtubule nucleation in vitro by stabilizing early nucleation intermediates.
source: It has been shown that TPX2 can directly promote MT nucleation in vitro, by stabilizing early nucleation intermediates (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: Early microtubule nucleation intermediates may share some common features with microtubule ends, possibly resembling a curved, GTP-rich, sheet-like structure.
source: While the structural nature of these intermediates is poorly understood, we hypothesize that they may share some common features with MT ends, possibly resembling a curved, GTP-rich, sheet-like structure (Chrétien et al., 1995; Guesdon et al., 2016; Voter and Erickson, 1984; Wang et al., 2005) (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on citations to published literature (Chrétien et al., 1995; Guesdon et al., 2016; Voter and Erickson, 1984; Wang et al., 2005).

claim: By slowing down GTP hydrolysis, TPX2 would allow early nucleation intermediates to have more time to grow and transform into elongating microtubules.
source: By slowing down GTP hydrolysis and therefore the premature transition to an unstable GDP state that is prone to depolymerization, TPX2 would allow the early nucleation intermediates to have more time to grow and transform into elongating MTs (Roostalu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on inference from structural observations and citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 may promote the formation of nucleation intermediates by bridging two short protofilaments and facilitating their lateral association.
source: In addition, given the flexible character of the linker between its two MT-binding elements, TPX2 may promote the formation of nucleation intermediates by bridging two short PFs and facilitating their lateral association, even before the final lateral curvature between PFs is established within the closed, cylindrical MT lattice (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the structural features of TPX2 binding.

claim: TPX2 is likely to stabilize protofilaments longitudinally because the ridge bridges across the tubulin interdimer interface along the protofilament.
source: Furthermore, given that the ridge bridges across the tubulin interdimer interface along the PF, TPX2 is also likely to stabilize PFs longitudinally.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural observation that the ridge bridges the interdimer interface.

claim: TPX2's effect on both lateral and longitudinal contacts might provide a structural explanation for why TPX2 directly promotes microtubule formation and stability so efficiently.
source: This effect on both lateral and longitudinal contacts might thereby provide a structural explanation for why TPX2 directly promotes MT formation and stability so efficiently.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural observations about TPX2 binding across multiple interfaces.

claim: Other parts of the TPX2 molecule can affect microtubule nucleation indirectly via other interaction partners such as Aurora A, γTuRC and augmin.
source: Besides the ridge and wedge motifs, that our results have identified as critical contributors to TPX2-dependent MT nucleation, other parts of the TPX2 molecule can affect MT nucleation indirectly via other interaction partners such as Aurora A, γTuRC and augmin (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Bayliss et al., 2003; Pinyol et al., 2013; Scrofani et al., 2015; Tsai and Zheng, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Bayliss et al., 2003; Pinyol et al., 2013; Scrofani et al., 2015; Tsai and Zheng, 2005).

claim: There is increasing evidence that TPX2 enhances the activity of γTuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation either indirectly or directly.
source: There is increasing evidence that TPX2 enhances the activity of γTuRC-dependent MT nucleation either indirectly (Pinyol et al., 2013) or directly (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pinyol et al., 2013; Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).

claim: TPX2 may bind in a similar manner to the interface between the γ-tubulin surface of γTuRC and the first tubulin layer, thereby directly promoting the templating activity of γTuRC.
source: In the light of the new binding mode of TPX2 observed here in the context of a MT, it is tempting to speculate that TPX2 may bind in a very similar manner to the interface between the γ-tubulin surface of γTuRC and the first tubulin layer, that is at the γ-tubulin/first α-tubulin interface, thereby directly promoting the templating activity of γTuRC in addition to stabilizing interdimer tubulin-tubulin contacts in the MT wall, as discussed above.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed binding mode of TPX2.

claim: Importin binding to TPX2 competes with microtubule binding of the central part of TPX2.
source: Therefore, importin binding to TPX2 competes with MT binding of the central part of TPX2, explaining previous observations with purified proteins (Roostalu et al., 2015), preventing TPX2 from stabilizing MTs and from promoting their nucleation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural overlap between importin-binding site and MT-binding elements, and citation to published literature (Roostalu et al., 2015).

claim: The microtubule contact sites in the wedge and ridge of TPX2 appear to be conserved only in organisms where a role of TPX2 for chromatin-dependent microtubule nucleation has been reported.
source: The observation that the MT contact sites in the wedge and ridge of TPX2 appear to be conserved only in organisms, such as vertebrates, where a role of TPX2 for chromatin-dependent MT nucleation has been reported (Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Vos et al., 2008) and not where TPX2 does not seem to be involved in this pathway (Hayward et al., 2014; Ozlü et al., 2005) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggests that this binding mode is distinctly responsible for Ran-GTP-regulated effects of TPX2 on MT nucleation and stability.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature.

claim: The TPX2 binding mode is distinctly responsible for Ran-GTP-regulated effects of TPX2 on microtubule nucleation and stability.
source: The observation that the MT contact sites in the wedge and ridge of TPX2 appear to be conserved only in organisms, such as vertebrates, where a role of TPX2 for chromatin-dependent MT nucleation has been reported (Gruss et al., 2001; Gruss et al., 2002; Vos et al., 2008) and not where TPX2 does not seem to be involved in this pathway (Hayward et al., 2014; Ozlü et al., 2005) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggests that this binding mode is distinctly responsible for Ran-GTP-regulated effects of TPX2 on MT nucleation and stability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the sequence conservation analysis and functional studies.

claim: The findings provide a mechanistic explanation of how the Ran-GTP gradient is coupled to microtubule nucleation and stabilization during mitosis.
source: Hence, our findings provide a mechanistic explanation of how the Ran-GTP gradient is coupled to MT nucleation and stabilization during mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural findings showing overlap between importin-binding and MT-binding sites.

claim: Through a novel binding mode involving small, flexibly linked structural motifs, TPX2 binds across longitudinal and lateral interfaces between tubulin subunits in the microtubule lattice promoting the association between tubulin subunits.
source: Through a novel binding mode involving small, flexibly linked structural motifs, TPX2 binds across longitudinal and lateral interfaces between tubulin subunits in the MT lattice promoting the association between tubulin subunits (Figure 6, top right and bottom right).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural findings from cryo-EM.

claim: TPX2-binding motifs allow the discrimination between nucleotide states in the microtubule lattice, possibly also slowing down GTP hydrolysis and the transition to a compacted GDP-microtubule lattice.
source: At the same time, TPX2-binding motifs allow the discrimination between nucleotide states in the MT lattice, possibly also slowing down GTP hydrolysis and the transition to a compacted GDP-MT lattice (Figure 6, bottom left).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural observations about lattice parameter changes and binding preferences.

claim: The new binding mode of TPX2 might contribute to stimulating γTuRC-mediated microtubule nucleation, in combination with indirect effects of TPX2 mediated by other interaction partners.
source: The new binding mode might also contribute to stimulating γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation, in combination with indirect effects of TPX2 mediated by other interaction partners.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed binding mode.

claim: Similar molecular mechanisms may be shared among a group of nuclear proteins that are activated upon nuclear envelope breakdown and function as spindle assembly factors in mitosis and meiosis.
source: Similar molecular mechanisms may be shared among a group of nuclear proteins that are activated upon nuclear envelope breakdown and function as spindle assembly factors in mitosis and meiosis.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning extrapolating from the TPX2 findings to other proteins.
